content: By the end of 2014, a total of 26 substances, including 16 pesticides, were listed in the annexes of the relevant international conventions. The most current list of these substances can be accessed on the official website of the convention. Many of these chemicals are also included under the Rotterdam Convention. Article 3 of the convention outlines strict prohibitions on chemicals listed in Annex A, requiring contracting parties to eliminate their production, use, import, and export. It also specifies restrictions on the production and use of chemicals listed in Annex B. However, imports of these chemicals for environmentally sound disposal are exempted. Specific exemptions for production and use are also allowed for certain chemicals in Annexes A and B, such as those used for disease vector control under specific conditions. Consequently, parties to the convention must implement national-level bans on the production and use of most chemicals listed in Annexes A and B. The convention also establishes requirements for the management of persistent organic pollutant (POP) stockpiles and wastes. The Basel Convention, which came into force in 1992, regulates the international movement of hazardous wastes, including obsolete pesticides and by-products or waste products from pesticides. While not specifically targeting pesticides, it is a valuable tool for governments to prevent the dumping of hazardous waste, such as obsolete pesticides, within their borders, especially in cases where governments lack the capacity to manage such waste in an environmentally sound manner. The convention defines hazardous wastes as those falling under categories in Annex I and exhibiting characteristics listed in Annex III. Annex I includes wastes from the production, formulation, and use of biocides (pesticides), while Annex III covers substances or wastes that can cause death, serious injury, or harm to human health through ingestion, inhalation, or skin contact, as well as those with delayed or chronic effects, including carcinogenicity. Under the Basel Convention, parties may prohibit the import of hazardous wastes or specific types of hazardous waste shipments. Exporting states are required to provide prior written notification to the importing state and obtain written consent before moving hazardous wastes across borders. The Montreal Protocol addresses substances that deplete the ozone layer, including the pesticide methyl bromide. Industrialized countries were required to eliminate methyl bromide production by January 2005, with certain exceptions for pre-shipment, quarantine, emergency uses, and critical-use exemptions where no feasible alternatives are available. Developing countries were granted a grace period but have agreed to phase out methyl bromide on an accelerated timeline. These exemptions are intended to be temporary and strictly limited. Several International Labour Organization (ILO) conventions address the safety and health of workers exposed to chemicals, including pesticides, particularly in agriculture. The C184 Safety and Health in Agriculture Convention, adopted in 2001 and effective in 2003, aims to close gaps in national legislation that often fail to protect agricultural workers from occupational health risks. Many workers exposed to pesticides, especially informal laborers, are not covered by existing legislation. The ILO Convention No. 182 on the Worst Forms of Child Labour, adopted in 1999, identifies work likely to harm the health, safety, or morals of children, including pesticide application, as a worst form of child labor. This is particularly concerning due to children's increased vulnerability to the toxic effects of pesticides. The Agriculture Convention imposes responsibilities on employers, strengthens workers' rights, and requires governments to develop coherent national policies on agricultural safety and health, establish inspection systems, and coordinate inter-sectoral efforts. The Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC) seeks to eliminate chemical weapons by prohibiting their development, production, stockpiling, and use. This has implications for the production, importation, and storage of large volumes of pesticides or obsolete stocks containing these chemicals. Non-binding international instruments, such as plans of action, declarations, codes of conduct, and technical standards, play a significant role in promoting international harmonization. The International Code of Conduct on Pesticide Management, adopted in 1985 and revised in 2013, provides a comprehensive framework for pesticide management throughout their life cycle. Although voluntary, the Code has been widely adopted by national governments and influences pesticide legislation. It includes specific recommendations for designing national pesticide laws and emphasizes integrated pest management. The Codex Alimentarius Commission (CAC), a joint body of the FAO and WHO, establishes harmonized food standards, including maximum residue limits (MRLs) for pesticides. These standards are recognized by the World Trade Organization (WTO) and are critical for ensuring food safety and facilitating international trade. Some governments have adopted Codex MRLs as legally binding standards to align national regulations with international consensus. The Globally Harmonized System of Classification and Labelling of Chemicals (GHS) provides a standardized framework for chemical hazard communication, including pesticides. It incorporates criteria for acute and chronic human toxicity and environmental toxicity, making it more comprehensive than the WHO Classification of Pesticides by Hazard. An increasing number of countries are adopting GHS as a binding standard through national legislation. Countries have various options for meeting their international legal obligations, including incorporating treaty obligations directly into national law, transposing international requirements into national legislation, or adjusting national laws to align with international instruments. Regional approaches to pesticide regulation, such as those in the European Union, West Africa, and the Andean Community, offer advantages like facilitating trade, sharing resources, and harmonizing standards. National pesticide legislation must be tailored to the country's legal framework and circumstances. A thorough review of existing laws and policies is essential to identify gaps, conflicts, and areas for improvement. This includes analyzing legislation on environmental protection, public health, occupational safety, food safety, and hazardous substance management. Stakeholder consultation and field information collection can provide valuable insights into the practical challenges of pesticide management and enforcement.
